newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Boots hands back cash, adds jobs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Boots hands back cash, adds jobs.

text.p: Britain's biggest chemist chain Boots Co Plc announced on Thursday a 400.5 million pound ($653.7 million) special cash payout to shareholders, plus the creation of 5,000 new retail jobs by the end of the century.

The retailer, also owner of Halfords car accessory stores and the Do It All home improvement chain, said it would share more of its cash riches with investors in the future unless it had a major acquisition in its sites.

Deputy chairman and chief executive Lord Blyth told Reuters in an interview that the company was "very cash generative". "Our shareholders have a very clear understanding from us that if we can't think of anything better to do with it we will give the cash back to them," he said.
He told a news conference that Boots had nothing on its radar screen at present that could be classified as a major acquisition.

The company, helped by the strong cash generation of its core business Boots The Chemists, has handed money back to shareholders on two other occasions via share buybacks; 511 million pounds in 1994 and 300 million in June last year.
Shareholders have received a total of 1.7 billion pounds from Boots over the last three years in dividends, buybacks and tax credits.
The payout, a special dividend of 44.2 pence a share, was announced along with an 8.7 percent increase in annual profits before tax and exceptional items to 536.2 million pounds.
The new jobs will come from the group's store expansion programme for 40 new Boots The Chemists shops a year and the same number of Halfords, costing in total around 70 million pounds annually.
The results and special dividend pleased investors.
"The stock has responded well to the special dividend," said one dealer. "At least they are not spending the money unwisely, they are giving it back to their shareholders."
The stock fell almost 30 pence initially to reflect the special dividend, which will be paid next week, but bounced back by the afternoon to stand 2.5 pence lower at 692.
"There were one or two areas of concern, particularly DIY, but the rest was really positive," said one retail analyst.

Retail analysts had speculated Boots might propose a special dividend this month ahead of the Labour government's first budget in July, which could remove the tax advantages on such payouts. But Boots denied that the timing was related to the budget.
Boots' core chain powered ahead as usual, producing a comparable store sales increase of 4.7 percent and increasing trading profits by 11 percent to 426.5 million pounds.
Boots' Do It All reduced losses from its ongoing business by about two thirds but Blyth admitted that the do-it-yourself market had been more competitive than expected
Blyth said the DIY market had proven much less attractive in overall terms and market leader B&Q, owned by Kingfisher Plc had become more powerful.
"It's been a much tougher situation than we expected."
Boots share of Do It All's losses last year was 6.9 million pounds, against 10.1 million. Last year Boots became sole owner of the chain when it bought out joint venture partner W.H. Smith Group Plc.
Boots also announced plans to go ahead with its Advantage "smart" loyalty card, after regional trials, but gave no details on the timing or scope of the launch.

Boots over-the-counter healthcare business Boots Healthcare International made a loss of 6.6 million pounds, down from 8.2 million last time. Blyth said Boots was not too worried about BHI making a profit at this stage as the emphasis focused on developing the business.
"Frankly we're not concerned about it making a bottom line profit at this point in time," he said in a telephone interview. "We're concerned about growing it as rapidly as we possibly can."

BHI, which develops and markets over-the-counter medicines, is in the process of launching products such as Nurofen pain relief across Europe. Last year Boots invested about 85 million stg in the business and expects to spend another 95 million in the current year.
